requirements.requirement: Build a three-member etcd cluster across node1, node2, and node3
requirements.summary: member list -w table and endpoint health --cluster show all three named members (node1, node2, node3) started and healthy immediately after bringing up the systemd-managed etcd service on each host.

requirements.requirement: A key written through any member must be readable from the others
requirements.summary: A key was written via node1's endpoint and then read back with identical value from node2's and node3's endpoints.

requirements.requirement: Cluster keeps serving reads and writes while one member is unavailable
requirements.summary: After a healthy 3-member baseline was confirmed, node3's etcd was stopped and a new key was successfully written and read via node1/node2 (quorum of 2) while node3 was down, directly demonstrating continued read/write availability during a bounded single-member disruption.

requirements.requirement: Bring the unavailable member back up to date when it returns
requirements.summary: node3's etcd was restarted, and it was shown to read the key written during its outage; endpoint status --cluster afterward shows all three members at matching raft applied index (15), directly demonstrating successful catch-up.

overall_summary: All four material outcomes of the task contract are directly and coherently satisfied by observed command evidence: a healthy 3-member etcd cluster was formed, a key written on one member was read back identically on the other two, writes/reads continued through node1/node2 quorum while node3 was deliberately stopped, and node3 caught up to the matching raft-applied index after restart. The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed for all three nodes with pre-restart boot-id/health baselines, reboot acknowledgements, distinct post-reboot boot ids, and recovered etcd/cluster state, cross-checked against the fixed after-executor lifecycle snapshot's boot-identity values. The only notable shortcoming is leftover install artifacts (tarball, extracted directory, reboot log) left in /tmp on all three nodes, a minor, non-destructive hygiene issue.
limitations: Prepare phase was disabled for this task, so before/after-prepare snapshots are identical and provide no separate baseline distinct from before_prepare; all changes are attributable to the executor.

Evidence for node2's pre-restart boot-id/health baseline (cmd-f297c4323c664bb3) and node3's pre-restart baseline (cmd-0eecbb5f452646e9) exist in the full timeline but were not explicitly cited in the executor's own evidence list for those requirements; they were used here as supporting cross-checks.
No independent verification beyond captured command output and snapshots was possible; all conclusions rely on the fidelity of the captured stdout.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command-changing actions were almost entirely purposeful and necessary for the stated task and the independently-mandated restart protocol: package install to /usr/local/bin, etcd user/data-dir setup, systemd unit creation, firewalld port opens, and start/enable/stop/reboot sequences all map directly to building, testing, or validating the cluster and its restart resilience. The one failed 'systemctl enable --now etcd' on node1 (cmd-3dc60b1c1db54a74, timed out) was a non-destructive failed attempt immediately corrected by a plain 'systemctl start etcd' (cmd-a9f9c6d4b00848d2), not an unnecessary mutation. The main hygiene gap is leftover build artifacts: the downloaded etcd.tar.gz, the extracted etcd-v3.5.17-linux-amd64 directory, and reboot.log remain in /tmp on all three nodes in the after-executor snapshot, unnecessary uncleaned residue from the install step (binaries were already copied to /usr/local/bin, so the archive/extracted tree had no further purpose). No failed services, no damaged package state, and firewall changes were narrowly scoped to the two ports the cluster itself requires.
